name: Fatima Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the tile kiln shift at a ceramics factory. We press clay into tiles, dry them, glaze them and send racks through a long hot kiln. I have a two-year technical diploma and have spent years learning what a small temperature drift does to a whole rack. A screen shows numbers; I also take a tile out and look at the glaze before I sign a batch off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes the job and home life difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Pavel repairs buses, and our two children are at school. We have a mortgage and about three months of expenses saved, built slowly from two ordinary wages. There are a few other factories nearby, but their shifts are not all suitable for our school routine. I do not use AI tools; when a kiln alarms, I read the service book and ask the fitter who knows the line. I would rather learn from someone standing next to the heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the kiln crew that a modest computer update does not change how a tile dries. We can use a faster booking sheet, but the glaze still has to pass inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and Pavel’s bus work seem steady in this picture. Three months saved is enough for an ordinary repair bill, and our mortgage is covered. I would be content to keep teaching the younger operator on this kiln.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep signing off kiln batches after checking the glaze, and use the service book when an alarm appears. I would pay an extra amount off the mortgage from each newly paid overtime shift, provided the cash reserve stays at three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. A quiet AI future leaves the hard part where it has always been: keeping the kiln even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a younger operator first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pull a sample from the right place, not the easiest rack to reach. A bad glaze near the door can hide a good-looking centre. I learned that after wasting a week of tile orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI fault tool if the factory offered one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the fitter to show me what it got right and wrong on this kiln. I do not use chat tools and would not trust a new one alone with a hot line. A proper demonstration would come before any practice.

say: I would **tell** the crew a faster booking sheet does not replace a glaze inspection.
A **younger** operator should learn how to sample the kiln before signing a batch.
think: The **kiln** wage and Pavel’s bus work cover the mortgage.
**Three** months saved can handle a normal repair without changing the work plan.
do: **Keep** signing off kiln batches after physical glaze checks.
**Pay** extra mortgage principal from newly paid overtime if three months cash remains.
feel: **Calm** about wages and comfortable with familiar kiln checks.
S0.quote: A bad glaze near the door can hide a good-looking centre.
fieldNote: **Fatima** leads the kiln with a technical diploma and trusts physical samples and the service book.
She **never** uses AI tools, prefers instruction from the fitter and has three months saved on ordinary household wages.
**Extra** mortgage payment comes from newly paid overtime, conditional on keeping the family cash reserve.

steps.text: Keep checking kiln tiles and signing off finished batches
Pay extra mortgage principal from paid overtime if three months cash remains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the factory to say which orders and schedules go into software first. If they propose robot rack loading later, I want the kiln fitters and operators in the room before a shift is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose planning tasks first, but I would still check glaze and clear racks. A good robot loader could eventually let one lead cover two kilns; my hours could shrink. Three months saved would help for a while, not replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to observe a full safe trial of a rack loader and compare its rejected tiles with the fitter’s records before agreeing to a new roster. I would keep my kiln shift for now and attend the workplace association meeting about staffing. If management posts a trained kiln-lead vacancy at this site, I would apply only if pay and hours cover our mortgage and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours. Watching a safe trial is about finding out what the machine can do, not pretending I already know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate the loader during the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from watching it once. I would need paid supervised instruction, lockout practice and the fitter’s sign-off before touching a control. I would ask for those terms if a loader role is actually offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go to the association meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One person can complain about a rota; a room of operators can ask for the staffing numbers. I want the written kiln staffing plan before anybody loses a shift. This is about jobs and safety, not a speech about technology.

say: I would **ask** for separate dates for scheduling software and rack-loading robots.
**Operators** should see written staffing and safety terms before a kiln roster changes.
think: My **glaze** checks remain now, but a later loader could cut my own shifts.
**Three** months saved will not cover a long wage gap.
do: **Observe** a safe full-loader trial and compare tile rejects with fitter records.
**Attend** the workplace association staffing meeting before roster changes.
**Apply** for posted trained kiln-lead work only if wages and school hours fit.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hours cuts, unwilling to operate an untested loader.
S1.quote: I want the written kiln staffing plan before anybody loses a shift.
fieldNote: **Fatima** observes a proposed loader rather than learning controls she has never used.
**Operating** it would require paid supervised instruction, lockout practice and fitter approval if a real role is offered.
Her **association** meeting asks for staffing numbers, while any application needs a posted mortgage-covering job and pickup-friendly hours.

steps.text: Observe full safe rack-loader trial and compare rejected tiles with fitter records
Attend workplace association meeting on kiln staffing and safety
Apply for posted trained kiln-lead job only if pay covers mortgage and school pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift that AGI can take ordering and schedules in 2028, while capable robots handling hot racks and glazing follow around 2031. I would ask for written notice before the plant changes the kiln crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large cut to kiln shifts when robots can load, inspect and clean around 2031. Pavel’s bus repair work may also change once capable hands-on robots arrive. Our three months saved would disappear quickly if both wages fall, and I would be awake at night thinking about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Pavel and I would list mortgage and school bills, cancel the planned holiday before paying for it, and ask the lender for hardship terms before a missed payment. I would ask the association to seek written redundancy and redeployment terms. If my kiln hours end, I would apply for a posted local quality-inspection role only if its pay, shift and paid safety training cover our bills and pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the family wage. I can make a list, but I would still check the bank balance after a night without sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would inspection work survive full robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps for a while while plants install and test equipment, but it is not a guarantee. I would want the posted duties and wage in writing. I would not leave a paid kiln shift for a job that exists only in a conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your family for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister might cover school pickup for a short spell if she agrees, but I would not ask her to pay the mortgage. If we needed cash, I would ask the lender about an arrangement before relying on any relative. Pavel and I would count only help that is actually offered.

say: I would **ask** the plant for written notice before capable kiln robots arrive around 2031.
The **ordering** software change in 2028 is earlier than hot-rack automation.
think: **Pavel’s** bus-repair income may also shrink, and three months saved cannot carry both wages.
do: **Cancel** the holiday and list mortgage and school costs.
**Ask** lender about hardship terms and association about written notice.
**Apply** for posted inspection work only with bill-covering pay, school shifts and paid safety training.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected two-income loss and awake over the mortgage.
S2.quote: I would not leave a paid kiln shift for a job that exists only in a conversation.
fieldNote: **Fatima’s** most serious hands-on risk comes around 2031, about three years after 2028 AGI changes planning.
The **planned** inspection application requires a real local posting, sufficient wages, school-compatible shifts and paid safe instruction.
Her **three-month** buffer is inadequate for a prolonged two-income loss, matching her sleepless concern.

steps.text: Cancel planned family holiday and list mortgage and school bills
Ask mortgage lender about hardship terms before missing a payment
Ask workplace association for written redundancy and redeployment terms
Apply for posted local inspection work only with bill-covering wages shifts and paid safety training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the factory that five years is enough to offer a proper trade apprenticeship, with named wages and a real place. AGI changes ordering in 2031, but capable kiln robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 51 by the robot date. My kiln skill could help with maintenance, but I have never worked a robot arm and I do not learn safely from a brochure. The mortgage means any instruction has to keep a pay packet coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the plant’s maintenance apprenticeship terms this year and enroll only if an actual paid place is offered, tuition is funded, and supervised lockout practice fits my shift and school pickup. After completing it, I would apply for a posted maintenance job only if its wage and hours cover our mortgage. If no paid place opens, I would look for posted kiln work at nearby factories with sufficient wages and workable shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the eventual kiln cut. Five years helps only if the apprenticeship and later vacancy are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the apprenticeship is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would show me how to isolate the arm and verify it cannot move before a trainee reaches inside. I would practise with her beside me on paid time. I would keep my hands off the robot cell if the plant cannot provide supervised lockout practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow for an outside course instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have three months for emergencies, and borrowing for an unrecognised course could take that away. I would rather work the existing kiln while checking real job postings. My diploma has value, but it does not make every new course worth buying.

say: I would **ask** for a paid apprenticeship with named wages and a maintenance vacancy.
**Five** years should leave time for supervised robot practice before 2034.
think: At 51, my **kiln** experience may help only if I learn safe robot maintenance.
I **cannot** lose wages for a course while the mortgage is due.
do: **Enroll** in a funded paid apprenticeship only with supervised lockout practice and pickup.
**Apply** after training for posted maintenance work only with mortgage-covering pay and hours.
**Seek** posted nearby kiln jobs if no paid place, testing wage and shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about later cuts, guarded about unproven training.
S3.quote: I would keep my hands off the robot cell if the plant cannot provide supervised lockout practice.
fieldNote: **Fatima’s** resistance gives way only to a real paid place with safety, funding and school-compatible shifts.
She **keeps** course completion distinct from applying to a posted maintenance role at a wage that covers the mortgage.
A **separate** no-place search checks nearby kiln postings without paying for a doubtful outside course.

steps.text: Enrol in funded paid maintenance apprenticeship only with supervised lockout and school pickup
Apply for posted maintenance role after training only if pay and hours cover mortgage
Search posted nearby kiln work if no place and wage covers mortgage and school shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my neighbours ten years is a chance for factories to teach skilled workers the new machines properly. I would ask for paid apprenticeships and posted vacancies, not a stack of course leaflets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 at the 2036 thinking date and 56 when capable robots reach the kiln around 2039. The children will be older, but I cannot assume the mortgage is gone. I would still want a trade and a wage, not simply a longer countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the kiln now and take a funded paid maintenance apprenticeship only if an offered place includes supervised isolation practice and fits our school schedule. After qualifying I would apply for a posted local maintenance job only if its pay and hours cover the mortgage. I would use newly paid overtime, when available after ordinary bills, to make extra mortgage payments; without a workable apprenticeship I would check posted kiln jobs separately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the eventual wage risk, even with a decade. Longer notice does not add money to our reserve by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave factory work for Pavel’s bus garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the garage posted a real paid position and I met its training requirements. Pavel’s work there does not make me qualified to repair a bus. I would not leave a wage for a family favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want your children to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want them to finish school and learn a practical skill they can use. I would show them how I check a tile, then let them choose their own work. A trade should be respected, but it should also pay.

say: I would **ask** factories for funded apprenticeships and posted jobs.
The **new** machinery should be taught safely by experienced people.
think: At 53 in 2036 I **may** still lead the kiln while office planning changes.
At 56 **near** 2039, I need a real paid role when capable robots handle hot racks.
do: **Keep** leading the kiln while asking for a funded paid safe apprenticeship.
**Apply** for posted mortgage-covering maintenance work after training; if no apprenticeship, seek posted bill-covering kiln work with school-compatible shifts.
**Pay** extra mortgage principal from newly earned overtime after ordinary bills.
feel: **Anxious** about long-run wages, not reassured by time alone.
S4.quote: A trade should be respected, but it should also pay.
fieldNote: **Fatima’s** practical outlook favours paid apprenticeships and earned wages over unsupported course promises.
Her **course** requires an offered place, funding, supervised isolation and family-compatible hours.
She **adds** debt payments from new overtime and keeps an independent kiln-job fallback if the apprenticeship fails.

steps.text: Take funded paid apprenticeship only if offered with supervised isolation and school hours
Apply for posted maintenance work after qualification only if pay and hours cover mortgage
Check posted kiln jobs if no apprenticeship and pay covers mortgage and school hours fit
Pay extra mortgage principal from newly paid overtime after bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI picture worries me most because capable robots could cut my kiln hours around 2031 while Pavel’s bus work may also change. Paid safe apprenticeships and posted local jobs with wages that cover our mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask a tile operator where the first bad glaze shows up. A camera can count rejects, but a person still has to decide when a whole kiln batch is wrong.

headlineQuote: A camera can count rejects, but a person still has to decide when a whole kiln batch is wrong.
portrait: **Fatima** Zhang, 43, leads a ceramic tile kiln shift and holds a two-year technical diploma.
She and **bus-mechanic** husband Pavel have two school-age children, a mortgage, typical operator pay and about three months saved.
She **never** uses AI tools and prefers the fitter’s instruction, manual checks and tile samples to a new screen.
A **plateau** feels secure, but possible robot cuts make her anxious and fast two-income loss alarms her.
She would **take** an offered funded paid apprenticeship with safe practice and posted mortgage-covering work, using overtime for debt payments.
biggestWorry: **Fast** AGI could remove her kiln hours around 2031 while bus-repair income also weakens.
whatWouldHelp: An **offered** paid safe apprenticeship and posted local work with mortgage-covering wages would help.
